title: What Is JavaScript?
objective: Understand what JavaScript is and how Code Forge runs the code you write.

sourceAlignment.title: JavaScript Crash Course
sourceAlignment.author: Nick Morgan
sourceAlignment.note: Adapted for Code Forge's in-browser runtime — no local installation. Lesson prose and exercises are original Code Forge material.

paragraphs: JavaScript is the programming language every web browser understands natively. It started as the language that makes web pages interactive, and today it also runs outside the browser — on servers, in apps, almost everywhere — but Code Forge focuses on the language itself first.

Normally, trying JavaScript means opening a browser's developer console or installing a separate runtime like Node.js. Code Forge skips that step: the editor on this page runs your JavaScript directly, so the code you write executes the moment you press Run.
Like most programming languages, JavaScript reads your code from top to bottom and runs it in that order. The order you write your lines in is the order they happen.
explanation.rule: JavaScript runs your code one line at a time, from top to bottom, exactly as written.

examples.title: Order Matters
examples.note: Each line runs in order. Swapping the second and third lines would cool the blade before it was ever struck.

checks.question: In what order does JavaScript execute the lines in a file?
options: Top to bottom, in the order they're written.
In a random order each time.

feedback.correct: Correct — JavaScript executes your code top to bottom, in the order you wrote it.
feedback.incorrect: JavaScript reads a file from the first line to the last, running each one as it goes.

assignment.title: Light the Forge
assignment.brief: Write lightTheForge() using console.log() to output exactly one line: Forge lit.
requirements: Use console.log() exactly once inside the function.
The logged text must be exactly: Forge lit.

hints: console.log(...) is how you print a value to the output.
Put the exact text "Forge lit." inside the parentheses, in quotes.
Match the punctuation exactly: a period at the end, no extra spaces.
The function needs to be called — lightTheForge(); — for anything to happen.
